title: Mertwig's Maze and the Satanic Panic
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j50kYrWuR6U

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens by cheerfully noting that the surest way to grow a young channel is a discussion of a 1988 game nobody cares about, then delivers something rather more personal than a look at TSR and Tom Wham's *Mertwig's Maze*.

He grew up in the 70s and 80s as the child of two ordained Christian ministers — liberal, open-minded, and absolutely immovable on one point: no Dungeons & Dragons. He sets that against the Satanic Panic, recommending Lawrence Wright's *Remembering Satan*, and traces the machinery of it: Jack Chick's tracts, the West Memphis Three, an obsession so arithmetically absurd it implied sixty thousand sacrificed infants a year. Conan was fine. Forgotten Realms was fine. Only the words on the box mattered. He bought *Mertwig's Maze* believing its cartoonish Wham art would pass, it fell out of his bag, his mother read "Advanced Dungeons & Dragons," and he had to return it to the shop.

Twenty years later he bought it again. It is, he concedes, not actually very good — a roll-and-move race — but two ideas stuck. Other players hold and play the encounters against you. And certain spaces lift your character off the main board onto little sub-maps with their own rules, a device that has shaped every game he has ever tried to design.

----

Which forbidden or unobtainable game from your childhood ended up larger in your memory than it ever was on the table?
